mainTopic: רבה's reason for the מודה במקצת oath, שמואל's reading of oaths to a minor and to הקדש, and the new משנה about items excluded from oaths, double payment and the watchman laws.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the discussion of a ברייתא about a son who claims his late father's loan. The גמרא explains that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the רבנן argue about רבה's idea: a debtor is not brazen enough to deny a debt to his creditor's face, so the Torah makes a מודה במקצת swear. The two sides disagree about whether that also holds in front of the creditor's son. The גמרא then defends reading the משנה like רבי אליעזר בן יעקב by telling apart a certain claim from an uncertain one. שמואל offers a different reading: the oath 'to a minor' or 'to הקדש' is a creditor's oath, taken in order to collect from a minor's property or from consecrated property. The גמרא shows why each of these teachings is needed, and it limits רב הונא's rule about a dying man to that case. A new משנה then lists slaves, documents, land and הקדש as items that are left out of oaths, double payment and the watchman laws. The same משנה also brings the opinions of רבי שמעון and רבי מאיר, and a rule that an oath requires a clear amount. The גמרא derives the double-payment exclusions from a כלל ופרט וכלל and explains why there is no four-or-five payment. It begins to bring a ברייתא for the watchman rule, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Every partial admission is a claim of others plus his own admission
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that what makes this case special is unclear, because all cases of מודה במקצת involve a claim by someone else and an admission by the defendant.
steps.simpleTranslation: But all the other cases are also a claim made by others together with the defendant's own admission!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is attacking the ברייתא's wording. The ברייתא says 'sometimes' a person swears on his own claim, which makes this case sound unusual, but every מודה במקצת case looks exactly like this one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In every partial-admission case, the plaintiff makes a claim (טענת אחרים) and the defendant admits part of it (הודאת עצמו). So it is unclear why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב presents this case as something special with the word 'sometimes'. The גמרא needs a new explanation of what the מחלוקת is really about.

keyTerms.meaning: A claim made by someone else (the plaintiff)

phrases.english: All of them also
are a claim of others and his own admission!

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוּלְּהוּ נָמֵי טַעֲנַת אֲחֵרִים וְהוֹדָאַת עַצְמוֹ נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of the ברייתא's phrase 'an oath on his own claim'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's framing of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's case as an unusual case ('sometimes').
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every partial-admission oath already involves someone else's claim and the defendant's own admission. So this case is no different, and the special framing seems pointless.

steps.title: The argument is about רבה's reason for the partial-admission oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the מחלוקת depends on רבה's principle: a debtor is not brazen enough to deny a debt completely in front of his creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they argue about רבה's idea. רבה said: Why did the Torah say that one who admits part of a claim must swear? Because there is a presumption that a person is not brazen in front of his creditor. This debtor really wants to deny the whole debt, and he doesn't deny it only because he is not brazen in front of his creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up its earlier approach and offers a new explanation. The two sides argue about how far רבה's principle reaches, so the גמרא first lays out what רבה said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה explains the logic behind the oath. A debtor would really like to deny everything, but he can't bring himself to lie completely to the face of the person who lent him money. That is why he admits part of the debt, and this half-admission makes him suspect.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits part of the claim
A presumption about how people normally behave
Acts brazenly (literally, makes his face bold)

steps.whyThisMatters: רבה's חזקה, that a person is not brazen in front of his creditor, is the classic explanation for why a מודה במקצת must swear. It comes up again and again across ש״ס.

phrases.english: Rather, they disagree about the idea of רבה
as רבה said:
For what reason did the Torah say
that one who admits part of the claim must swear?
It is a presumption that a person is not brazen
in front of his creditor.
And this one wants to deny all of it,
and the fact that he did not deny it
is because he is not brazen
in front of his creditor;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by moving the מחלוקת to a new basis.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-explaining the basis of the מחלוקת
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case seemed to be about swearing 'on one's own claim', which made it no different from any other partial admission.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is really about whether רבה's 'not brazen' principle also applies in front of the creditor's son.

steps.title: Why the debtor holds back, and why the Torah imposes an oath
steps.stepSummary: רבה goes on: the debtor would like to admit everything, but he holds back part of the debt to buy time until he has money. The Torah puts an oath on him to push him to admit the whole thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he really wants to admit all of it to him. The reason he didn't admit is that he is pushing the creditor off, thinking: 'Until I have money, and then I will pay him.' So the Merciful One said: put an oath on him, so that he will admit all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה finishes his explanation. The debtor isn't a real thief; he is only stalling, so the Torah uses an oath to pressure him into telling the whole truth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because he is not brazen, the debtor would like to admit everything. He holds part back only to delay payment until he has money. The oath works as pressure: faced with swearing falsely, he will admit the full amount.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבה, a מודה במקצת swears because he admitted part (he is not brazen in front of his creditor) but held part back (he is stalling). The oath pushes him to admit everything.

phrases.english: And he wants to admit all of it to him,
and the fact that he did not admit to him
is that he is pushing him off,
thinking: until I have money
and then I will pay him;
and the Merciful One said: put an oath on him,
so that he will admit all of it to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבה's statement, which began in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah imposes an oath on a מודה במקצת to pressure a debtor who is stalling into admitting the full debt.

steps.title: Applying רבה's principle to the creditor's son
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds that a debtor is not brazen even in front of the creditor's son, so this is a normal partial admission and he swears. The רבנן hold that he would be brazen in front of the son, so admitting part makes him a משיב אבידה, and he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds: it makes no difference whether it is the creditor himself or his son, the debtor is not brazen. Therefore he is not a משיב אבידה. The רבנן hold: he is not brazen only in front of the creditor himself, but in front of the son he would be brazen. So since he was not brazen, he is a משיב אבידה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now uses רבה's principle to explain both sides of the ברייתא. The whole argument turns on whether the debtor would dare to deny the debt completely in front of the creditor's son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the debtor isn't brazen even in front of the son (רבי אליעזר בן יעקב), his partial admission is the usual 'half-honest' kind, and he must swear. If he would normally be brazen in front of the son (רבנן), then admitting anything at all is pure honesty, like returning a lost object, and he is exempt from the oath.

keyTerms.meaning: In front of his son (the creditor's son)
One who returns a lost object; here, someone who volunteers an admission out of honesty and is exempt from swearing

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides accept רבה's reason for the oath. They disagree only about whether 'not brazen' also applies to the creditor's son. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says yes, so the debtor swears; the רבנן say no, so he is a משיב אבידה and exempt.
steps.confusionAlert: משיב אבידה here does not mean he returned an actual lost object. It means his admission is treated like an honest volunteer's act, so he is freed from the oath.

phrases.english: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב holds:

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא בּוֹ וְלָא שְׁנָא בִּבְנוֹ – אֵינוֹ מֵעֵיז,
phrases.english: it makes no difference with him or with his son, he is not brazen,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the original lender, and 'his son' is the lender's son who is now making the claim.

phrases.english: and therefore he is not a returner of a lost object.
And the רבנן hold:
it is in front of him that he is not brazen,
but in front of his son he is brazen;
and since he was not brazen, he is a returner of a lost object.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב סָבַר: לָא שְׁנָא בּוֹ וְלָא שְׁנָא בִּבְנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבה's principle from steps 2-3 to the two opinions in the ברייתא, completing the answer to step 1.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The מחלוקת is about whether the 'not brazen' presumption extends to the creditor's son. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says it does, so the debtor swears; the רבנן say it does not, so his partial admission makes him a משיב אבידה and he is exempt.

steps.title: Can the משנה really follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that the משנה follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, because an earlier clause says that a defendant who admits half of a debt claimed for a father is exempt as a משיב אבידה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really explain the משנה like רבי אליעזר בן יעקב? The earlier clause teaches: 'My father had a hundred in your hand.' 'You only have fifty dinars in my hand.' He is exempt, because he is like someone returning a lost item!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the earlier explanation that the משנה's 'oath to a minor' follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. It points to an earlier clause of the same משנה that sounds exactly like the רבנן's view, not his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier clause, a son claims his late father's money and the defendant admits half. The משנה exempts him as a משיב אבידה. That is the רבנן's reasoning, so how can the same משנה follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב?

keyTerms.meaning: Can you really set it up as (following this opinion)?
Someone returning a lost item, who is exempt from an oath

phrases.english: Can you really set it up
according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב?!
But the earlier clause teaches:
"My father had a hundred in your hand,"
"You only have fifty dinars in my hand"
– he is exempt,
because he is someone returning a lost item!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי מָצֵית מוֹקְמַתְּ לַהּ כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that steps 2-4 have clarified רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's view, the גמרא challenges the earlier reading that the משנה follows him, using the משנה's earlier clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: Explaining the משנה according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The earlier clause exempts a partial admission to a son as משיב אבידה, which is the רבנן's view, so the משנה seems to follow the רבנן.

steps.title: The difference is whether the claimant says 'I am certain'
steps.stepSummary: The earlier clause is a case where the son did not claim with certainty; our case is where he says 'I am certain.'
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he did not say 'I am certain.' Here, he said 'I am certain.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by splitting the two cases. Both clauses can fit רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier clause, the son is not sure of his claim, so even רבי אליעזר בן יעקב agrees the defendant is a משיב אבידה. In our case the son claims with certainty, so admitting part is a normal מודה במקצת and requires an oath.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not change his view here. The answer only says the earlier clause is a different case, where the claimant is unsure.

phrases.english: There, it is where he did not say "I am certain,"
here, it is where he said "I am certain."

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם דְּלָא אָמַר בָּרִי לִי, הָכָא דְּאָמַר בָּרִי לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (uncertain claim vs. certain claim)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The earlier clause and our case are the same situation, so the משנה must follow the רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The earlier clause is an uncertain claim, where all agree he is a משיב אבידה; our case is a certain claim, where רבי אליעזר בן יעקב requires an oath.

steps.title: שמואל: the oath is taken in order to collect from a minor or from הקדש
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains 'an oath to a minor' differently: a creditor swears in order to collect from a minor's property, and 'to הקדש' means to collect from consecrated property.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: 'To a minor' means in order to collect from a minor's property. 'To הקדש' means in order to collect from הקדש property.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל offers a whole new way to explain the משנה's words 'an oath to a minor and to הקדש.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here it is not a defendant swearing because of a claim. Instead, the creditor swears to the minor heir or to הקדש that he was not repaid, so that he can collect from their property.

phrases.english: שמואל said:
"To a minor" – in order to collect from a minor's property,
"To הקדש" – in order to collect from הקדש property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different explanation of the משנה instead of the רבי אליעזר בן יעקב approach.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The oath 'to a minor' and 'to הקדש' is the creditor's oath, needed to collect from a minor's property or from consecrated property.

steps.title: Why teach the oath to collect from orphans twice?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to שמואל: another משנה already teaches that one collects from orphans' property only with an oath, so why repeat it?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'To a minor, to collect from a minor's property' — we already learned it: From the property of orphans, one collects only with an oath! Why do I need two?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's explanation. If he is right, the משנה is repeating a law taught elsewhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A different משנה already says one collects from orphans only with an oath. If our משנה just means the same thing, the two teachings are duplicates.

phrases.english: "To a minor" to collect from a minor's property
– we already learned it:
From the property of orphans
one collects only with an oath!
Why do I need two?

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנֵינָא: מִנִּכְסֵי יְתוֹמִים לֹא יִפָּרַע אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבוּעָה! תַּרְתֵּי לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's explanation in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's explanation of 'an oath to a minor.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If it means collecting from orphans with an oath, it repeats another משנה, and the משנה does not repeat itself for nothing.

steps.title: The repetition teaches that the rule covers adult and minor orphans
steps.stepSummary: The repetition teaches אביי קשישא's rule: the 'orphans' of that law are adults, and certainly minors, both for the oath and for collecting only from poor land.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches us like אביי קשישא, who taught: The orphans they spoke of are adults, and needless to say minors; both for the oath and for collecting from the poorest land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two teachings are not duplicates. Together they show the rule covers adult orphans and minor orphans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One teaching says 'orphans' and ours says 'a minor.' Together they show that the oath rule applies to adult orphans, and of course to minors. The same is true for the rule that one collects from orphans only from the poorest land.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us
אביי the Elder, an early teacher

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל explains 'an oath to a minor' as the creditor's oath to collect from a minor's property. The repetition is not extra: it teaches, like אביי קשישא, that the rules of oath and poorest land apply to adult orphans and certainly to minors.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the practical rule that collecting from any orphans, adult or minor, needs an oath and is only from the poorest land.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us
– like אביי קשישא;
as אביי קשישא taught:
The orphans they spoke of – are adults,
and needless to say minors;
both for the oath and for the poorest land.
phrases.notes: Collecting from orphans' property comes only from their lowest-quality land.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן כִּדְאַבָּיֵי קַשִּׁישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each teaching adds something: together they cover adults and minors
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה just repeats the law about collecting from orphans.
steps.terutzMaskana: The two teachings together show that adult orphans are included, and minors certainly, for both the oath and the poorest land.

steps.title: Why teach the oath for collecting from הקדש?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the second half of שמואל's explanation. Another משנה already teaches that collecting from liened property needs an oath, and הקדש should be no different.
steps.simpleTranslation: As for 'to הקדש', meaning to collect from consecrated property: we already learned that from liened property one collects only with an oath. What difference does it make whether the property is liened to a regular person or to the Most High?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks the second half of שמואל's explanation ('to הקדש'). It says that this law is already taught elsewhere, so it should not need to be repeated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 asked the same kind of question about the 'minor' part of שמואל's reading. Here the claim is that consecrated property is simply one more kind of liened property, and the rule for liened property already requires an oath. If so, there is nothing new in saying it about הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: Property that was given to the בית המקדש
Property that is tied to a debt and was later sold to someone else
An ordinary person, as opposed to הקדש
'The Most High.' Another way of saying הקדש

phrases.english: 'To הקדש' means: to collect from consecrated property
phrases.notes: This quotes שמואל's explanation from step 7.

phrases.english: We already learned: from liened property
one may collect only with an oath;
so what difference is it to me if it is liened to an ordinary person,
or if it is liened to the Most High?
phrases.notes: 'The Most High' here means הקדש, property that belongs to the בית המקדש.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנֵינָא: מִנְּכָסִים מְשׁוּעְבָּדִים לֹא יִפָּרְעוּ אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Does the same thing as step 8, but now aimed at the 'הקדש' half of שמואל's reading
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's reading that 'to הקדש' means swearing in order to collect from consecrated property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה about liened property already covers this law. Liened to a person or liened to הקדש makes no difference, so repeating it is unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have thought nobody plots against הקדש
steps.stepSummary: The repetition was needed. Without it, we might have said the oath exists only because people plot against ordinary buyers, and nobody would plot against הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was necessary. You might have thought that the oath applies to an ordinary person, because people do plot against an ordinary person. But with הקדש, where people do not plot against הקדש, maybe no oath is needed. So the משנה teaches us that an oath is needed there too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the הקדש case adds something new. It shows that the fear of plotting, which is the reason for the oath, applies even against הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath for collecting from liened property exists because of a worry. The lender and borrower might team up, for example with a note that was already paid, to take land from the buyer. One might think nobody would cheat the בית המקדש, so the oath would not apply there. The משנה tells us the worry, and the oath, apply to הקדש as well.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It was necessary.' The repeated teaching adds something
'You might have thought.' This introduces the mistaken first idea
A secret plan by two people to cheat a third
'It teaches us.' This brings the real point

phrases.english: It was necessary;
it might have entered your mind to say:

phrases.aramaic: הֶדְיוֹט הוּא דְּאָדָם עוֹשֶׂה קְנוּנְיָא עַל הֶדְיוֹט;
phrases.english: it is with an ordinary person that the oath applies, since a person plots against an ordinary person;
phrases.notes: The plot means the lender and borrower team up, maybe with a note that was already paid, to take land from the buyer.

phrases.english: but with הקדש,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאֵין אָדָם עוֹשֶׂה קְנוּנְיָא עַל הֶקְדֵּשׁ –
phrases.english: since a person does not plot against הקדש, no oath would be needed
so it teaches us that an oath is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10 by showing that the הקדש case adds a new point
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא (showing that the repetition was needed)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Nobody plots against הקדש, so no oath is needed to collect from it
steps.terutzMaskana: People are suspected of plotting even against הקדש, so an oath is needed
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the next question. Does the fear of plotting really apply to הקדש?

steps.title: רב הונא says nobody plots against הקדש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this using רב הונא. He believes a dying man who gave all his property to הקדש and then admits a debt, because nobody plots against הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב הונא say: a dying man who gave all his property to הקדש and said 'So-and-so has a maneh in my hand' is believed, because the presumption is that a person does not plot against הקדש!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling of רב הונא. It seems to say the opposite of what step 11 just said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 said that people do plot against הקדש. רב הונא uses the exact idea step 11 had rejected, 'nobody plots against הקדש', to believe a dying man's admission of a debt. The two seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is dangerously ill and may die soon
A coin worth one hundred זוז (dinars)
A presumption that we assume is true

phrases.english: But didn't רב הונא say:
a dying person who consecrated all his property,
and said: 'So-and-so has a maneh in my hand,'
he is believed,

phrases.aramaic: חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם עוֹשֶׂה קְנוּנְיָא עַל הֶקְדֵּשׁ!
phrases.english: since there is a presumption that a person does not plot against הקדש!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 11
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 11 that people do plot against הקדש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב הונא accepts as a presumption that no one plots against הקדש. That goes against the reason step 11 gave for requiring an oath.

steps.title: A dying man gains nothing, but a healthy man might
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא's rule is only about a dying man, who has nothing to gain by lying. With a healthy person we do worry about plotting.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: that applies to a dying person, because a person does not sin when he gains nothing. But with a healthy person, we certainly worry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by limiting רב הונא's rule to a dying person. This keeps the oath for collecting from הקדש in normal cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody sins unless he gets something out of it. A dying man gains nothing for himself by cheating הקדש, so we believe him. A healthy man could share in the profit of a plot, so the worry stays and the oath is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'These words apply.' This limits a rule to a certain case
A person does not sin when he himself gains nothing
We worry; we take the risk into account

steps.whatToRemember: Collecting from הקדש needs an oath, because a healthy person might plot even against הקדש. רב הונא's rule, that we believe him, is only for a dying man who gains nothing.

phrases.english: They said: that applies only to a dying person,
since a person does not sin when he gains nothing himself;
but with a healthy person,
we certainly worry about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12 by limiting רב הונא's rule to a dying person
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule to its own case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא's presumption applies to everyone
steps.terutzMaskana: It applies only to a dying man, who gains nothing. A healthy person may plot, so he must swear.

steps.title: משנה: four kinds of property left out of oaths and fines
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה lists slaves, documents, land and consecrated property. These have no Torah oath, no double payment, no four-or-five payment, and special rules for watchmen.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: These are items about which one does not swear: slaves, documents, land and consecrated property. They have no double payment and no payment of four and five. An unpaid watchman does not swear, and a paid watchman does not pay.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists four kinds of property that are left out of several Torah money laws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עבדים, שטרות, קרקעות and הקדשות are still real property. They are just treated differently from regular movable items in these laws. With them there is no Torah oath for a partial admission, no כפל for a thief, and no ד' וה' payment. An unpaid watchman does not swear, and a paid watchman does not pay if the item is lost or stolen.

keyTerms.meaning: Double payment that a thief pays
Paying four or five times, when a thief slaughters or sells a stolen sheep or ox
An unpaid watchman / a paid watchman

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean these items are not property, or that there is no claim over them at all. It means only that these specific Torah laws, like the oath, כפל and the watchman rules, do not apply to them.

phrases.english: MISHNA: And these are items
about which one does not take an oath:
slaves and documents
and land and consecrated property.
With them there is no double payment
and no payment of four and five,
an unpaid watchman does not swear,
a paid watchman does not pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of שמואל ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עבדים, שטרות, קרקעות and הקדשות have no Torah oath, no כפל, and no ד' וה'. An unpaid watchman does not swear over them, and a paid watchman does not pay for them.

steps.title: רבי שמעון: Consecrated Items the Owner Must Replace Get an Oath
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון says that if a person is responsible to replace a consecrated item, people swear about it. If he is not responsible, they do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: Consecrated items that the owner is responsible to replace, people swear about them. Consecrated items he is not responsible to replace, people do not swear about them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with רבי שמעון, who disagrees with the flat rule that הקדש never gets a Torah oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the משנה said there is no oath on consecrated property. רבי שמעון makes a split. If the owner must replace the animal when it is lost, the loss really falls on him, so it counts as his own money and an oath applies. If he does not have to replace it, it belongs fully to הקדש and there is no oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Consecrated items (such as animals set aside for the בית המקדש)
Responsibility to replace something if it is lost

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
Consecrated items that he is responsible for,
phrases.notes: For example, he promised to bring an offering and then picked an animal. If that animal is lost, he still owes an offering.

phrases.english: one takes an oath about them,
and those he is not responsible for,
one does not take an oath about them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: קֳדָשִׁים שֶׁחַיָּיב בְּאַחְרָיוּתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה from Step 14 and adds a split to its rule about consecrated property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Consecrated items the owner must replace get an oath. Items he need not replace do not.

steps.title: רבי מאיר and the Sages Argue About Vines Loaded With Grapes
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says some things attached to the ground are not treated like land, so a claim about loaded vines needs an oath. The חכמים say anything attached to the ground counts as land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: Some things are in the ground but are not treated like land, and the Sages disagree with him. For example: 'I gave you ten vines loaded with grapes to guard,' and the other says, 'There were only five.' רבי מאיר requires an oath. The Sages say: anything attached to the ground is like land.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a מחלוקת between רבי מאיר and the חכמים about whether grapes still on the vine count as land, which has no Torah oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land does not get a Torah oath. רבי מאיר holds that ripe grapes ready to be picked are really treated like loose fruit, so the partial admission (five out of ten) triggers an oath. The חכמים say that as long as something is attached to the ground, it counts as land, so there is no oath.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי מאיר does not say the vines themselves are not land. He says the ripe grapes on them are treated like loose produce, so this is an exception inside the category of attached things.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
There are things that are in the ground
but are not treated like land;
and the Sages do not agree with him.
How so?
'I handed you ten vines loaded with grapes,'
and the other one says: 'There were only five.'
Rabbi Meir requires an oath,
and the Sages say:
anything attached to the ground
is treated like land.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: יֵשׁ דְּבָרִים שֶׁהֵן בְּקַרְקַע וְאֵינָן כְּקַרְקַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה and looks at the edges of the 'land' category from Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, a claim about loaded vines requires an oath. According to the חכמים, anything attached to the ground is land and has no oath.

steps.title: An Oath Applies Only to a Claim With a Clear Amount
steps.stepSummary: An oath is required only when the claim has a clear size, weight or number. A vague claim like 'a full house' does not lead to an oath, but a dispute about 'up to the ledge' versus 'up to the window' does.
steps.simpleTranslation: One takes an oath only about something counted by measure, weight or number. For example: 'I gave you a full house' or 'I gave you a full pouch,' and the other says, 'I don't know; whatever you left, take.' He is exempt. If one says 'it was full up to the ledge' and the other says 'up to the window,' he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new rule: a claim must have a clear amount before an oath can apply. It then gives one case that is exempt and one that is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'A full house' or 'a full pouch' has no clear amount, and the defendant does not admit to any specific amount either, so there is no oath. Once each side names a clear level, such as the ledge or the window, the claim and the admission are measurable, so the oath applies.

keyTerms.meaning: A ledge sticking out of the wall

steps.whatToRemember: A Torah oath needs a claim with a clear amount. A vague 'it was full' is not enough, but 'full up to this mark' is.

phrases.english: One takes an oath only about something
that is by measure, by weight, or by number.
How so?
'I gave you a full house'
phrases.notes: He means a house full of produce.

phrases.english: or 'I gave you a full pouch,'
and the other one says: 'I don't know,
but whatever you left here, you may take'
he is exempt.
If this one says 'it was full up to the ledge'
and that one says 'only up to the window,'
he is obligated to take an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין אֶלָּא עַל דָּבָר שֶׁבְּמִדָּה וְשֶׁבְּמִשְׁקָל וְשֶׁבְּמִנְיָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the משנה with a general rule about which claims can lead to an oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath applies only to a claim with a clear amount. 'A full house' is exempt; 'up to the ledge' versus 'up to the window' is liable.

steps.title: Where Do We Learn That These Items Have No Double Payment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the source that slaves, documents, land and הקדש are excluded from תשלומי כפל.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Double payment, from where do we learn it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by asking for the Torah source behind the משנה's rule that these items do not get תשלומי כפל. This sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14's משנה listed four kinds of items with no double payment. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק excludes them.

keyTerms.meaning: Double payment: a thief, or a watchman who falsely claims the item was stolen, pays twice its value

phrases.english: Gemara
Double payment, from where do we derive it?
phrases.notes: He is asking where we learn that the four items in the משנה are left out of double payment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the משנה into the גמרא and asks for the source of the first rule in Step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק shows that slaves, documents, land and הקדש are excluded from double payment?

steps.title: The ברייתא Reads the Verse as General, Detail, General
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the double-payment פסוק as a general phrase, then a list of details, then another general phrase. This structure will be used to define which items are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught: 'For every matter of trespass' is a general statement; 'for an ox, for a donkey, for a sheep, for a garment' is a detail; 'for any lost thing' goes back and makes a general statement again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by starting to quote a ברייתא that breaks the פסוק into general, detail and general. This sets up the conclusion about what is included, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the Torah writes a general phrase, then specific examples, then another general phrase, we include only things similar to the examples. The examples here are all movable items that have their own value, and that will be the reason slaves, documents, land and הקדש are left out.

keyTerms.meaning: A general statement in a פסוק
A specific detail or example in a פסוק
It went back and made a general statement again
A matter of wrongdoing, a disputed claim of theft

steps.whyThisMatters: This כלל ופרט וכלל structure is the tool that will define exactly which items get double payment.

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
'For every matter of trespass' is a general statement;
'for an ox' and 'for a donkey'
and 'for a sheep' and 'for a garment' is a detail;
'for any lost thing': it went back and made a general statement again.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן: עַל כׇּל דְּבַר פֶּשַׁע כְּלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of Step 18 by quoting a ברייתא on the פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is the double-payment פסוק, read as כלל ופרט וכלל. The conclusion of the reading comes next.

steps.title: Only items like the listed details are included
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא applies the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל. Only things that are movable and are worth money in themselves get double payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: A general phrase, then details, then another general phrase means you include only things like the details. The details are movable things that are worth money in themselves. So anything movable that is worth money in itself is included.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its reading of the double-payment פסוק. It sets the rule for what counts: movable things that are worth money in themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 19 the פסוק was shown to have a general phrase, a list, and another general phrase. The rule is that the list sets the limits: you include only items that share its features. The listed items (ox, donkey, sheep, garment) are all movable and have real value of their own, so those two features become the test.

keyTerms.meaning: A general phrase, then a list of details, then another general phrase; a rule for reading the תורה
The object itself is worth money

steps.whyThisMatters: This two-part test (movable, and valuable in itself) is what knocks out each item in the next step.

phrases.english: A general phrase, a detail, and a general phrase –
phrases.notes: This is the pattern in the double-payment פסוק, שמות 22:8, that was set up in the last step.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט;
phrases.english: you include only things like the detail;
just as the detail is clearly
a movable thing whose body is worth money,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כׇּל דָּבָר הַמִּטַּלְטֵל וְגוּפוֹ מָמוֹן.
phrases.english: so too, anything movable whose body is worth money.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reading of the פסוק that step 19 began.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Double payment applies only to movable items that are worth money in themselves.

steps.title: Land, slaves, documents and הקדש are excluded
steps.stepSummary: Using the test, the ברייתא leaves out land (not movable), slaves (compared to land), and documents (not valuable in themselves). It leaves out הקדש because the פסוק says 'his neighbor.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Land is left out because it does not move. Slaves are left out because the תורה compares them to land. Documents are left out because, even though they move, the paper itself is not worth money. הקדש is left out because the פסוק says 'his neighbor.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא runs each item through the new test and shows why it does not get double payment. This answers the question from step 18.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land fails the 'movable' test. Documents pass the 'movable' test but fail the 'worth money in itself' test, since they only prove a debt. Slaves are left out because the תורה compares them to land. הקדש is left out for a different reason, the word רעהו, because it belongs to the בית המקדש and not to a fellow person.

keyTerms.meaning: Slaves (here, a Canaanite slave, עֶבֶד כְּנַעֲנִי)
His neighbor, meaning a fellow person

steps.whatToRemember: Movable + worth money in itself = double payment. Land, slaves and documents fail that test, and הקדש is left out because of the word רעהו.
steps.confusionAlert: הקדש is not left out by the movable/valuable test. Many הקדש items are movable and valuable. It is left out only because of the word רעהו.

phrases.english: Land is excluded – because it is not movable;
slaves are excluded – because they were compared to land;
documents are excluded –
because even though they are movable,
their body is not worth money;
phrases.notes: The paper is worth almost nothing. It only matters because it proves a debt.

phrases.english: consecrated property – 'his neighbor' is written.
phrases.notes: The פסוק says he pays double 'to his neighbor,' which means a person, not the בית המקדש.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the test from step 20 to each excluded item.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Land, slaves, documents and הקדש do not get תשלומי כפל.

steps.title: Why no four-or-five payment for הקדש?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: there is no double payment and no four-or-five payment for these items. It asks for the reason behind the four-or-five part.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said there is no double payment and no four-or-five payment. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next phrase of the משנה and asks why stealing a הקדש animal and then slaughtering or selling it does not bring the payment of four or five. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The double payment was already explained. But the four-or-five payment comes from a separate פסוק about animals, so one might think it still applies to הקדש animals. The גמרא wants to know what removes it.

keyTerms.meaning: Four or five times the value, paid for stealing a sheep or ox and then slaughtering or selling it

phrases.english: And not double payment
and not four or five.
What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the double payment to the four-or-five payment in the same משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the four-or-five payment does not apply to stolen הקדש animals.

steps.title: The תורה said four or five, not three or four
steps.stepSummary: The four-or-five payment includes the double payment inside it. Without the double, it would be only three or four, which the תורה never set.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תורה said a payment of four or five, not a payment of three or four.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that since there is no double payment for הקדש, the four-or-five payment cannot work either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The four or five times are counted as including the double payment. Once the double is taken away for הקדש, all that would be left is a three-or-four payment. The תורה never set such a payment, so there is no extra payment at all.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the תורה

steps.whatToRemember: The four-or-five payment depends on the double payment. No כפל means no ארבעה וחמשה.

phrases.english: The Merciful One said a payment of four or five,
and not a payment of three or four.
phrases.notes: Without the double payment that is built into it, four or five would shrink to three or four.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Since the four-or-five payment includes the double, and there is no double for הקדש, only a three-or-four payment would be left. The תורה never set such a payment.

steps.title: Source that a שומר חנם does not swear
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that a שומר חנם does not swear about these excluded items, and asks for the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: An unpaid watchman does not swear. Where do we learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next rule in the משנה and asks for its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a שומר חנם who says the item was lost must swear. The משנה says he is free of that oath for land, slaves, documents and הקדש. The גמרא wants a פסוק-based source for that exclusion.

keyTerms.meaning: Where are these things learned from?

phrases.english: An unpaid watchman does not swear.
From where are these words?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next rule of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that a שומר חנם does not swear about land, slaves, documents and הקדש.

steps.title: Introducing a ברייתא as the source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins its answer by bringing a ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is about to quote a ברייתא that will give the source asked for in step 24.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words דתנו רבנן mean the answer will come from a teaching of the תנאים. The content of that ברייתא comes next.

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer will come from a ברייתא, quoted next.
